take: Dated Brent surging above $120 whilst ICE Brent slips toward $101 is the standout dislocation, signalling a genuine physical squeeze in the North Sea and wider Atlantic Basin that should keep prompt crude and distillate cracks bid even as the flat price looks conflicted. The G7's agreement to release up to 100 million barrels of emergency diesel and crude over four months is the second theme, and its transmission into freight is straightforward: more government barrels moving into a tight fuel market means additional tonne-miles and sustained demand for product tankers, reinforced by Kuwait Oil Tanker Company suffering its second VLCC strike in four days and a projectile attack briefly disrupting loading at Yanbu. On positioning, the squeeze narrative is corroborated by VLCC secondhand values now exceeding newbuild prices — the "death zone" — which tells you owners are pricing in prolonged dislocation rather than a normalising market, whilst the U.S. rig count fell again this week even as the EIA forecasts record 2026 crude output of 13.8 million b/d, a divergence worth monitoring. The cross-market link to watch is the diesel complex versus bunker: with European diesel stocks being tapped and 21 LNG cargoes exiting Hormuz in September — the highest since the Iran war began but still well below pre-war levels — gasoil strength should keep VLSFO and MGO bunker premiums supported, feeding directly into dry bulk and tanker voyage economics. Over the next 24 hours, watch whether Dated Brent holds above $120 and how the market digests the first tranche of the G7 release, plus any further Hormuz security headlines, since the WTI whipsaw between improving Gulf flows and returning Middle East risk is the clearest signal of which way this breaks.

items.title: Public companies produce most U.S. crude oil and natural gas
items.summary: Publicly traded companies represent a tiny share of the total number of companies producing crude oil and natural gas in the United States, but they make up a large share of U.S. production. In 2025, publicly traded companies accounted for just 2% of about 12,000 oil and natural gas producers but produced 68% of the crude oil and natural gas in the Lower 48 states.

items.title: What goes into diesel prices?
items.summary: The price of distillate fuel oil, often sold as diesel, is driven by the price of crude oil, retail margins, distribution costs, taxes, and crack spreads, the indicator we use for refining margins. Tight global supplies of distillate fuel oil and elevated crude oil prices have driven prices higher in recent months.
